changelog: Replace C7 to address the primary finding: soften the absolute predicate–argument preservation rule so it avoids creating many micro‑fragments in very short‑latency contexts and instead describes what a good dense cut looks like (prefer cohesive remainders, avoid trailing single‑word fragments).
findings: The prompt treats predicate–argument preservation as an absolute rule across all latency regimes, preferring to avoid any cut that separates verbs/auxiliaries from arguments; in very short-latency sentences this drives many tiny fragments elsewhere and lowers overall H_set in the ≤3/≤5 bins.

The prompt undervalues isolating sentence‑initial small function words or discourse markers as standalone pieces; separating an initial article/discourse token often yields a following chunk that is more coherent to translate and raises joinable quality.

The prompt does not sufficiently penalize cuts inside coordinate lists or enumerations; splitting mid‑enumeration often severs the list's internal cohesion and causes mistranslation when pieces are joined.

diagnosis.why: Softening C7 made the instruction ambiguous in short‑latency contexts: the model moved some cuts earlier (splitting prepositional phrases, pulling apart verb–object/adjunct sequences and producing one‑word fragments) which reduced H_set for small bins, while giving a tiny net gain on long pieces where the softer rule allowed useful additional cuts.
diagnosis.lesson: When softening predicate–argument constraints, make it explicit that the model must not shift cuts earlier in very short‑latency pieces so as to create isolated single‑word fragments or split tight verb‑argument/PP units.
